title: Chunking strategies, and why they decide retrieval quality
story:
A chunk is the unit of retrieval, which means it is also the unit of evidence. Whatever you cut the documents into is what the system can find, and what it finds is all the answer can be built from. You are deciding what the model will be allowed to know, before anyone has asked anything.

That framing is the whole lesson, and it puts chunking in a different category from the tuning knob it is usually treated as.

Start with what goes wrong at each end, because the two failures look nothing alike. Cut too large and the passage that matches your question arrives surrounded by text about something else. The match itself is diluted, since most of what was compared to the query is irrelevant, and the window fills with words that cost money and attention and carry no information for this question. Cut too small and you get the opposite: the sentence that matches is severed from the thing that made it mean anything. A line saying it must be renewed every year is useless when the subject was named two paragraphs earlier. A row of numbers is unreadable without the header. A clause is ambiguous without the section it sat under.

Both failures are quiet. The system returns something, the answer reads fluently, and nobody sees the paragraph that would have changed it.

There is a third failure that is structural rather than a matter of degree, and it is the one to design against. A fact that spans a boundary cannot be retrieved by either half, because neither half contains it. Cutting the document did not merely split the evidence, it destroyed it, and no amount of better matching recovers what is no longer present in any single unit. Overlapping the cuts is the cheap insurance against this: you pay in storage, which is the resource you have most of.

From there the practical rules are short, and they follow from the same idea.

Cut along the structure the document already has. A document has been organised by someone — sections, headings, rows, steps — and those boundaries are where meaning actually changes. A fixed character count is a boundary that lands where nothing in particular ends, and it will regularly fall between a heading and the thing it heads, or between a question and its answer.

Keep the context of the piece attached to the piece. The heading path, the document title, the section it belonged to — a small amount of text that tells a reader what they are looking at. It costs a little room in every chunk and it is what stops a retrieved fragment being uninterpretable.

Store what a chunk's neighbours are, so you can widen after retrieval rather than before. Retrieval works better on small units, because the match is not diluted; reading works better on larger ones, because the context is present. Retrieve narrow and expand what you found, and you get both.

And then the part people skip. You cannot judge a chunking strategy by looking at the chunks. They always look reasonable. The only test is whether the passages you need come back for the questions you actually get, which means you need a handful of real questions with the passages that should answer them written down, and you re-run that set whenever the strategy changes. Everything else is taste.

One more thing worth holding onto, because it saves an argument. There is no correct size in the abstract. The right unit depends on the questions you expect, and a question about a single value wants a small precise unit while a question about how something works wants a coherent whole. Choosing the chunk is choosing which questions the system is good at, and if your questions vary widely, that is an argument for storing them at more than one size rather than for finding the number that suits everything, because that number does not exist.

problem.name: Choosing the unit of retrieval
problem.shape: A body of text must be cut into pieces before it can be searched, and the pieces are what the answer gets built from.
tell: the retrieved passage is mostly about something else
the retrieved passage is missing the subject, the header, or the section it belonged to
an answer exists in the documents and no query brings it back
the pieces were cut at a fixed length with no regard for the document's structure
problem.move: Cut along the structure the document already has, attach the heading path to every piece, overlap the cuts so nothing that spans a boundary is destroyed, and record each piece's neighbours so you can retrieve narrow and expand afterwards.
problem.invariant: The system can only answer from what is contained in a single retrievable unit, so any fact that spans a boundary is unavailable to it no matter how good the matching is.
problem.breaks: There is no correct size in the abstract — the right unit depends on the questions expected, so a single setting cannot serve questions that want a precise value and questions that want a coherent explanation.

cost.time: smaller pieces mean more of them, so both indexing and search grow with the count
cost.space: overlap duplicates text on purpose, paying in storage to protect against a boundary destroying a fact
cost.beats: handing over whole documents, which buries the match and fills the window, and single sentences, which retrieve cleanly and cannot be interpreted

worked.problem: Why does the way text is cut up decide the quality of the answers?
worked.reasoning:
Because the piece is the unit of retrieval, and therefore the unit of evidence. The answer can only be built from what came back, and what can come back is whatever you cut.

The two obvious failures pull in opposite directions. Pieces that are too large dilute the match, since most of what was compared to the query is about something else, and they fill the window with text that costs money and carries nothing for this question. Pieces that are too small separate the matching sentence from whatever made it meaningful — the subject named two paragraphs earlier, the header above the row, the section the clause sat under.

What makes both dangerous is that they are quiet. Something is returned, the answer reads well, and nobody sees the passage that would have changed it.

The third failure is the one I design against, because it is structural rather than a matter of degree: a fact spanning a boundary is in neither half, so cutting did not split the evidence, it destroyed it. Better matching cannot recover what no unit contains. Overlapping the cuts is the cheap protection, paid in storage.

So the rules I follow are to cut along the structure the document already has, since a fixed character count lands where nothing ends and will fall between a heading and what it heads; to attach the heading path so a fragment is interpretable on its own; and to record each piece's neighbours so I can retrieve narrow, where the match is sharp, and expand afterwards, where the context is needed.

And I would not judge any of this by reading the pieces, because they always look reasonable. The test is whether the passages I need come back for the questions I actually get, which means keeping a handful of real questions with their expected passages and re-running them whenever the strategy changes.

problem.practice: Take a document you know well and ask a question whose answer sits across a section boundary. Cut the document at a fixed length, retrieve, and watch the answer come back confident and incomplete. Then cut it along its own headings with overlap and ask again. One afternoon of this is worth any amount of advice about sizes.

beats.broke: Cutting text at a fixed length puts boundaries where nothing ends, so facts get split across pieces and pieces arrive without the context that made them mean anything.
beats.fix: Cut along the document's own structure, attach the heading path, overlap the cuts, and record neighbours so retrieval can be narrow and reading can be wide.
beats.cost: Overlap duplicates text and more pieces cost more to index and search, and no single size serves every kind of question.

interview.q: Why does the way text is cut up decide the quality of the answers?
interview.trap: Treating it as a tuning parameter to be optimised once. The piece is the unit of evidence, so the cut decides which questions are answerable at all — and a fact spanning a boundary is destroyed rather than merely split.
interview.answer:
Because the piece is the unit of retrieval and therefore the unit of evidence: the answer can only be built from what came back, and what can come back is whatever you cut.

Too large dilutes the match, since most of what was compared to the query is about something else, and it fills the window with text that costs money and carries nothing. Too small severs the matching sentence from what made it meaningful — the subject named earlier, the header above the row, the section the clause sat under. Both failures are quiet: something comes back, the answer reads well, and nobody sees what was missed.

The failure I actually design against is structural. A fact that spans a boundary is in neither half, so cutting destroyed it rather than split it, and no improvement in matching recovers what no unit contains. Overlapping the cuts is the cheap insurance, paid in storage.

So: cut along the structure the document already has, because a fixed character count falls where nothing ends and will separate a heading from what it heads. Attach the heading path so a fragment can be interpreted alone. Record neighbours so retrieval can be narrow, where the match is sharp, and reading can be wide, where the context lives.

And I would not evaluate it by reading the pieces, which always look fine. The test is whether the passages I need come back for the questions I really get, which means keeping a small set of real questions with their expected passages and re-running it whenever the strategy changes.

takeaway: The chunk is the unit of retrieval and therefore the unit of evidence, so a fact that spans a boundary is destroyed rather than split — cut along the document's own structure, overlap the cuts, keep the heading attached, and judge the strategy only by whether the right passages come back for real questions.
